name: Abstract Factory
intent: Create whole families of related objects that are guaranteed to belong together, without naming their concrete classes.
scenario: A UI toolkit builds buttons and checkboxes. In the Light theme every widget must be Light, in the Dark theme every widget must be Dark, and the two must never be mixed.
problem: The form code creates a Button and a Checkbox. If it picks each widget's class separately, a Dark button can end up next to a Light checkbox. Every new theme means hunting down every place that creates widgets.
solution: Define a factory interface with one creation method per product (createButton, createCheckbox). Each theme implements it and returns only its own family. The client receives one factory and cannot accidentally mix families.
pain: Every widget needs its own if/else on the theme
Nothing prevents a Dark button next to a Light checkbox
A new theme means editing every creation site
The form knows every concrete widget class
benefits: The form receives one factory and asks it for widgets
A factory returns one consistent family, so mixing is impossible
A new theme is one new factory, no edits to the form
The form only knows the Button and Checkbox interfaces
whenToUse: Your code must work with several families of related products
Products from one family are designed to be used together
You want to swap the whole family in one place (theme, platform, database vendor)
whenNotToUse: There is only one family, or only one product type: Factory Method is lighter
Families rarely change and mixing is harmless
Adding a new product type is common: every factory then has to change
pitfalls: Adding a new product (a Slider) means editing the factory interface and every concrete factory
Many small classes: products times families
Often confused with Factory Method; Abstract Factory is a set of factory methods for related products
Needs a place to choose the concrete factory once, usually at startup

roles.label: Abstract Factory
roles.description: Interface with one creation method per product type.

roles.label: Concrete Factory
roles.description: Creates the products of one family.

roles.label: Product
roles.description: Interface for one kind of object in the family.

roles.label: Concrete Product
roles.description: A real widget belonging to one family.

quiz.question: A UI toolkit has LightButton, LightCheckbox, DarkButton and DarkCheckbox. Twelve screens each pick widgets with their own `if theme == dark` check, and a bug report shows a dark button beside a light checkbox. What is the best fix?
options: Make Button and Checkbox share a base class with a theme field that throws on a mismatch
Put the theme name in a shared constant and have the screens read it before building widgets
Scan each finished screen afterward and swap any widget that has the wrong theme
Give each screen one ThemeFactory, chosen once at startup, and ask it for every widget
quiz.explanation: One factory per theme can only return widgets of its own family, so mixing becomes impossible and screens stop knowing concrete classes. A shared constant still leaves twelve places that branch on it, and a post-hoc scan or runtime throw only detects the mix after it happened.

quiz.question: A toolkit uses an Abstract Factory with four theme factories (Light, Dark, HighContrast, Retro). The team adds a new Slider widget that must exist in every theme. What does that change involve?
options: Add one Slider class and register it in the form code that builds each screen, leaving the factories alone
Create a fifth SliderFactory that every existing theme factory calls whenever a slider is wanted
Add createSlider to the Light factory only and let the other three themes fall back to it at runtime
Add createSlider to the interface and to all four factories, with a Slider class for each theme
quiz.explanation: A new product type touches the abstract interface and every concrete factory, which is the known cost of this pattern. A single Slider class would give the other themes no matching slider, and falling back to Light would reintroduce mixed families.

quiz.question: A desktop app uses an Abstract Factory for themes. A user switches from Light to Dark while ten windows are open. The dev swaps the app's factory reference to DarkFactory and changes nothing else. What happens?
options: Every open window repaints in Dark, because widgets look up the factory each time they draw
Existing widgets stay Light while later ones are Dark, so families end up mixed on screen
Nothing changes until the app restarts, since the factory is only read once at startup
The first new window crashes, because a factory cannot be replaced after products exist
quiz.explanation: A factory only controls objects created after it is chosen. Already-built Light widgets keep their family, so new Dark ones appear next to them. A runtime switch needs the windows to rebuild their widgets from the new factory.
